subject: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square

messages.author: c89471eda5dca12c
messages.subject: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square
parts:
I am building a PA model using lavaan using a sample size of 63000 records with non-normal categorical binary and ordinal variables. 

Probably by this sample size, after the model estimation we obtained a high chi-square result and insignificant p-value.

So I would like to confirm some assumptions I got after reading some literature:
  • The X2 test is sensisitve by the large sample sizes and would be corrected, it the normality assumptions are not valid, using Satorra Bentler correction. 
  • If correct, in lavaan we can fix it using test="Satorra.Bentler" in lavaan ?

  • In Kline book (2015) page 80, the use of normed chi-­square (x2/df) is discourage because X2 is sensitive to sample size only for incorrect models; df has nothing to do with sample size and there were really never any “acceptable” clear-cut guidelines about maximum values of the normed chi-­square (e.g., < 2.0?—< 3.0?). 
  • So I have seem a lot of papers using this index. Should I use it when evaluating the quality of my model or not?

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square
parts:
Elias

Even with the satorra bentler correction the X2 is most likely to reject the null hypothesis.

There is no research that shows that the X2/df works, under any condition. I havent seen papers using it but they shouldnt.

For this assesing of model fit (quality) is recommended to use other fit indexes, such as CFI, TLI, RMSEA, gamma-hat, Mc. The function fitMeasures of lavaan and moreFitindices from semTools provide plenty of fit indexes. 

From research it shows that gamma-hat, RMSEA, and MC to have better behavior

You can check 

West, S. G., Taylor, A. B., & Wu, W. (2012). Model fit and model selection in structural equation modeling. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Handbook of Structural Equation Modeling (pp. 209-231). New York, NY: Guilford.

Fan, Xitao and Sivo, Stephen A.(2007) 'Sensitivity of Fit Indices to Model Misspecification and Model Types', Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42: 3, 509 — 529

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square
parts:
Elias,
  It is somewhat misleading to say that chi-square is sensitive to N.  It is not that the large N makes the chi-square inaccurate in some way.  However, you may have sufficient power to detect trivial discrepancies between the observed and implied moments.  The correction for non-normality is not related to having a large N and the chi-square is not in need of any correction for having a large N.

  My suggestion in such circumstances would be to pay special attention to the residuals in a correlation metric.  In the correlation metric, you can think about how big a difference in correlations is of any practical significance.  Then look at the residuals and see how many, if any, exceed that threshold.  If none do, then you can report that the chi-square indicated an overall difference but that all of the differences were too small to be of practical significance.

   What makes the ratio of chi-square to df interesting is that the df are the mean of the chi-quare distribution.  So, some of us take chi-square < df as a potential warning that a model is at risk for overfitting the sample.  However, given that the shape of the distribution changes with df, it is hard to give any meaningful interpretation to the ratio when it exceeds 1.

  Whatever you do, bear in mind that there are no universally accepted practices.  Kline's overview of model evaluation is very good, at least for those of us who take a holistic perspective on model evaluation.  When you report your results, clearly connect the dots between your conclusions and the evidence that you provide to support them.  Be sure to provide sufficient information that the reader can make his or her own independent evaluation.

Keith

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square
parts:
Elias,
I do not have any examples to offer.  I would recommend the discussion of residuals in the current edition of Rex Kline's SEM text.  Here is some illustrative code.


# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)


# View Residuals (documentation in the lavaan-class help file)
resid(fit, type='raw')
resid(fit, type='cor')
resid(fit, type='normalized')

# Extract unique correlation residuals
fitCorResiduals <- resid(fit, type='cor')$cor
fitCorResidualsUnique <- fitCorResiduals[lower.tri(fitCorResiduals, diag=TRUE)]

# View summary and stem-and-leaf plot
summary(fitCorResidualsUnique)
stem(fitCorResidualsUnique)

# Another plot option
plot(fitCorResidualsUnique[order(fitCorResidualsUnique)], pch=16,
  xlab='', ylab='Correlation Residual')
  abline(h=c(0, -.1, .1), lty=c(1,2,2))

# Flag residuals GT .1 or LT -.1 (choose your own threshold)
flaggedResiduals <- which(abs(fitCorResiduals) > .1, arr.ind=TRUE)
flaggedValues <- fitCorResiduals[flaggedResiduals]
flaggedRowNames <- rownames(fitCorResiduals)[flaggedResiduals[1:5,1]]
flaggedColNames <- colnames(fitCorResiduals)[flaggedResiduals[1:5,2]]
myFlaggedResiduals <- data.frame(flaggedRowNames, flaggedColNames, flaggedValues[1:5])
myResiduals[order(myFlaggedResiduals$flaggedValues),]
